title: Climate change has intensified Europe's risk of drought, scientists say
facts: A World Weather Attribution study found climate-driven heat intensified severe drought conditions across Europe.
Mariam Zachariah is a climate researcher at Imperial College London who co-authored the drought study.
The atmosphere can hold approximately 7% more water vapor for every 1 degree Celsius increase in temperature.
Global temperatures have warmed approximately 1.4 degrees Celsius since the pre-industrial period (1850–1900).
The Copernicus Climate Change Service recorded the hottest June in western European history in 2026.
Dominik Schumacher is a researcher at ETH Zurich who co-authored the European drought study.
The study found that extremely dry soil conditions are five times more likely in western Europe due to climate change.
Extremely dry soils are 11 times more likely in eastern Europe compared to a pre-industrial climate.
Atmospheric evaporative demand between April and June in western Europe was approximately 80 times more likely due to climate change.
Europe is recognized by scientists as the fastest-warming continent on Earth.
Countries from France to Romania implemented water restrictions and confronted parched rivers.
A major heatwave across western Europe in June 2026 caused thousands of excess fatalities.
Scientists utilized climate models and weather data to compare current drought levels with a world 1.4C cooler.
Spring rainfall levels across large areas of Europe were below historical averages.
Accelerated soil moisture evaporation during spring and summer increased wildfire susceptibility across European regions.
